でしょう.en: でしょう is the polite form. You want the casual form.
でしょう.es: でしょう es la conjugación formal. Tienes que usar la versión informal.
でしょう.fr: でしょう est la forme polie. On veut la forme familière.
でしょう.id: でしょう adalah bentuk sopan. Kamu memerlukan bentuk kasual.

でしょ.en: でしょ is the contracted polite form. You want the casual form + something more masculine.
でしょ.es: でしょ' es la conjugación formal acortada. Tienes que usar la versión informal + algo más masculino.
でしょ.fr: でしょ est la forme polie contractée. On veut la forme familière + quelque chose de plus masculin.
でしょ.id: でしょ adalah bentuk sopan yang disingkat. Gunakan bentuk kasual dengan nuansa yang lebih maskulin.

attributes.nuance_translation: A structure that casually highlights what the speaker thinks is probable, or is looking for agreement on.

attributes.body:
だろう is a conjugated form of だ, and can also be seen in the contracted form だろ (more casual). だろう expresses that the speaker thinks that something is true (assertion/expectation), and also that the listener would probably agree with them. This comes across like 'right?', or 'probably' in English.

だろう carries exactly the same meaning as でしょう (the polite equivalent). However, due to だ being more casual than です, だろう is also considered to be more casual/masculine than でしょう.

Caution

While だろう is usually used when the speaker has some sort of information that would support their assertion, it can also be used simply when the speaker 'feels' that something is true.

In this kind of sentence that expresses a 'feeling' or 'hunch', だろう comes across as quite low confidence. The speaker's tone of voice will often reveal how confident だろう is.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.description: でしょう / だろう in Japanese
Using 「でしょう」 and 「だろう」 to express strong amount of certainty (casual)
Difference between そうです、ようです、だろう and らしいです

attributes.body: まい and だろう are both used to express speculation, but they contrast in polarity. だろう indicates positive speculation or likelihood, as in 雨が降るだろう (It will probably rain), while まい expresses strong negative speculation or denial, as in 雨は降るまい (It probably won’t rain).

first_relatable.title: まい
first_relatable.meaning: Won't, Intend not to, Probably not

attributes.body: Both でしょう and だろう express conjecture (e.g., 'It's probably…') or seek confirmation when used with rising intonation in a question (e.g., 面白いでしょう？ or 面白いだろう？ = 'It's interesting, right?'). でしょう is more polite and used with strangers or those of equal or higher rank, while だろう is casual and blunt, used with close friends, family, and in informal settings.

だろう is a form of だ used when the speaker feels uncertain. It's often translated as 'probably,' 'I guess,' or '...right?' when asking a question. In contrast, ね is used to seek confirmation or agreement, often translated as '...isn't it?' These two can combine to express both uncertainty and confirmation, as in 面白いだろうね ('It's probably interesting, isn't it?').

だろう is a form of だ used to express mild uncertainty (like 'It's probably…') or to seek confirmation from the listener ('It's this, right?'). のではないだろうか is similar but expresses much less certainty, with a nuance of wondering or seeking confirmation or approval ('I wonder if it's…?').

second_relatable.title: のではないだろうか
second_relatable.meaning: I think ... isn't it?, It might be that..., Don't you agree?

attributes.body: かもしれない (polite form かもしれません) and だろう (polite form でしょう) are both casual phrases used to express uncertainty or possibility, but with different degrees of certainty. かもしれない is less certain, similar to 'maybe' or 'might,' while だろう expresses a higher degree of certainty, like 'probably' or 'I guess.'

だろう, in addition to expressing conjecture ('It's probably…'), can seek confirmation or agreement from the listener (e.g., 面白いだろう = 'It's interesting, right?'). じゃないか is more forceful and assertive, suggesting the speaker strongly believes something and expects agreement (e.g., 面白いじゃないか = 'It's interesting, isn't it!'). Both are casual forms and should be avoided in polite conversation.
